---
title: "Git and GitHub field guide"
subtitle: "The small set of ideas and commands used in POLI 210"
---

You do not need to master all of Git to succeed in this course. POLI 210 uses a
simple workflow: each assignment begins in a private GitHub repository, you
work on a local copy in RStudio, and you push a sequence of commits back to
GitHub. This page is the course reference for that workflow.

## What the tools are

| Term | Meaning in this course |
|---|---|
| **Git** | Software on your computer that records changes to files as a history of snapshots. |
| **GitHub** | A website that stores a remote copy of a Git repository and runs assignment checks. |
| **Repository** | A project folder together with its Git history. We often shorten this to **repo**. |
| **RStudio Project** | The local working folder you open through its `.Rproj` file. RStudio's Git pane gives you buttons for common Git operations. |
| **GitHub Actions** | The automated checks that run on GitHub after you push. |

Git and GitHub are related but not identical. Git works locally and can record
commits without an internet connection. GitHub stores the remote repository;
it only receives a local commit after you **push** it.

```text
GitHub: private remote repository and Actions
                  ^ push
                  |                 clone once / pull updates
                  |                           |
Your computer: edit -> save -> stage -> commit
```

::: {.callout-important title="Save, commit, and push are different"}
**Save** updates a file on your computer. **Commit** records a selected set of
saved changes in the local Git history. **Push** sends local commits to GitHub.
A saved answer is not submitted until its commit has been pushed.
:::

## Vocabulary for the homework workflow

- **Clone:** Make the initial local copy of a GitHub repository, including its
  history and connection back to GitHub. Clone once per assignment.
- **Diff:** A line-by-line view of what changed since the last commit. Green
  lines were added; red lines were removed.
- **Stage:** Select the saved changes that belong in the next commit. In
  RStudio, check a file in the Git pane to stage it.
- **Commit:** Record the staged changes as a local snapshot with a short
  message explaining the work.
- **Push:** Send local commits to the GitHub repository.
- **Pull:** Bring remote commits into the local repository. In an individual
  assignment this is usually needed only if the instructor has updated the
  repository or you edited it from another computer.
- **Working tree:** Git's name for the files currently in your local project
  folder.
- **`main`:** The single branch used for POLI 210 assignments. You do not need
  to create other branches.

## The course workflow

### Once for each assignment

1. Accept the private repository invitation from GitHub.
2. On GitHub, select **Code**, choose **HTTPS**, and copy the URL.
3. In RStudio, choose **File -> New Project -> Version Control -> Git**.
4. Paste the URL and clone into your local `Documents/POLI210` folder.
5. Open the project through its `.Rproj` file.

See [GitHub and RStudio workflow](github-rstudio.qmd) for the illustrated menu
sequence and authentication advice. Do not download the assignment as a ZIP
file; a ZIP does not include the Git history or the connection to GitHub.

### During every work session

1. Open the correct `.Rproj` file and confirm the project name in RStudio.
2. Run `git status` in the Terminal. If the working tree is clean and you need
   an instructor update, run `git pull --ff-only`.
3. Edit and save a small, meaningful part of the assignment.
4. Render the Quarto document and run the assignment's local check.
5. Inspect each changed file's diff in the Git pane.
6. Stage the files that belong together.
7. Commit with a descriptive message such as `Complete Part 2`.
8. Push, then inspect the newest run under GitHub's **Actions** tab.

Repeat the edit-to-push cycle several times. Small commits are easier to
understand and recover than one enormous final commit.

## Commands you will actually use

Run these in RStudio's **Terminal**, from the assignment's project folder. They
are Git commands, not R code, so do not enter them in the R Console.
The commands are the same on macOS and Windows; only the terminal prompt and
the way a full [file path](file-paths.qmd) is written may look different.

| Command | What it tells Git to do |
|---|---|
| `git status` | Summarize the current branch, saved changes, staged changes, and commits not yet pushed. This is the best first diagnostic command. |
| `git diff` | Show saved changes that have not been staged. RStudio's **Diff** button shows the same basic information. |
| `git diff --staged` | Show exactly what the next commit will contain. |
| `git add a1-reproducible-workflow.qmd` | Stage one file. For later assignments, substitute the actual filename. Checking a file in RStudio's Git pane does this too. |
| `git commit -m "Complete Part 2"` | Record the staged changes locally with a message. RStudio's **Commit** window does the same thing. |
| `git push` | Send local commits to GitHub. |
| `git pull --ff-only` | Bring down remote commits, but stop instead of creating an unexpected merge commit. |
| `git log --oneline -5` | Show the five most recent local commits. |
| `git remote -v` | Show which GitHub repository the local project is connected to. |

You may also see the command-line form `git clone REPOSITORY-URL`. In this
course, use RStudio's new-project menu to clone so that it creates and opens the
RStudio Project correctly.

::: {.callout-tip title="Read git status literally"}
- `Changes not staged for commit` means Git sees saved changes that are not yet
  selected for a commit.
- `Changes to be committed` means files are staged for the next commit.
- `Your branch is ahead of 'origin/main'` means you have local commits to push.
- `nothing to commit, working tree clean` means Git sees no uncommitted saved
  changes.
:::

## Common problems

### My change is not in the Git pane

Save the file, then run `git status`. Also confirm that you opened the correct
`.Rproj` file and edited the copy inside that project. See the
[file-path guide](file-paths.qmd) if you may have two copies of the assignment.

### GitHub does not show my latest work

A save or local commit does not update GitHub. Run `git status`, commit any
intended changes, and push. On GitHub, confirm that the newest commit message
matches the one you just made.

### Push was rejected or mentions `non-fast-forward`

Do **not** force-push. First run `git status`. If the working tree is clean, run
`git pull --ff-only` and read the result. If Git refuses or reports a conflict,
stop and send the instructor the exact message before trying more commands.

### I staged the wrong file

Uncheck it in RStudio's Git pane, or run:

```bash
git restore --staged FILENAME
```

This removes the file from the staging area without deleting your saved edits.

### The newest GitHub Action failed

Open the newest run, expand the failed step, and read the first useful error.
Confirm that the run used your newest commit. An Action failure does not erase
your work; it means the remote check found something to repair.

## Safety rules

- Work in the RStudio Project copy, not in a downloaded ZIP or a second copy.
- Do not edit the same assignment alternately in RStudio and GitHub's web
  editor; that creates two changing copies that must be reconciled.
- Do not run `git init` inside a cloned assignment.
- Do not use `git push --force`, `git reset --hard`, or delete the hidden `.git`
  folder. Ask for help before using a command that discards or rewrites work.
- Never commit passwords, access tokens, or other secrets.
- Before following a Git command from a web search or AI tool, make sure you
  understand what it changes. When uncertain, show the proposed command and
  current `git status` to the instructor first.

## Before you finish an assignment

- [ ] The Quarto document renders successfully.
- [ ] The local assignment check completes as expected.
- [ ] The diff contains your intended work and no secrets or accidental files.
- [ ] Your commits have descriptive messages.
- [ ] `git status` says the working tree is clean and the branch is up to date
      with `origin/main`.
- [ ] GitHub shows your newest commit and its newest Action run.

## Optional deeper references

The material above is sufficient for the normal POLI 210 workflow. If you want
more detail:

- GitHub's [About Git](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/using-git/about-git)
  explains version control, repositories, and how GitHub relates to Git.
- GitHub's [Getting changes from a remote repository](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/using-git/getting-changes-from-a-remote-repository)
  explains clone, fetch, and pull.
- [Happy Git and GitHub for the useR](https://happygitwithr.com) is the broader
  R-oriented tutorial previously used in this course. Its
  [Git commands chapter](https://happygitwithr.com/git-commands) is a useful
  extended reference, but most of the book goes beyond what you need for A1.
